sections.heading: Asking to see and speak of the cross rightly
sections.text: Father, make more room in my heart for what you have done. Stir up love in me where I am cold. Open my mouth, and give me honest words to say that your love shines most clearly at Calvary.
theological_themes: God awakens worship in a cold heart
The cross as the clearest display of divine love
Dependence on God even for worthy praise

scripture_references.connection: Paul points to Christ's death for sinners as the decisive demonstration of God's love, which directly supports the prayer's desire to see love shining at Calvary.
David asks God to open his lips so that praise can come from him. That fits the section's dependence on God to supply both affection and words for worship.

sections.heading: What you placed on your Son for me
sections.text: At the cross, you lifted the weight I could never carry and laid it on your Son. He stood in the place of sinners. He bore the curse I deserved. He was treated as sin for me, though he was holy, so that your justice would be satisfied and your mercy could reach me without denying who you are.
theological_themes: Christ bearing sin and curse for sinners
God's justice and mercy meeting at the cross

scripture_references.connection: This passage teaches that the sinless Christ was made sin for believers so that they might receive righteousness in him, grounding the prayer's language of exchange at the cross.
Paul says Christ redeemed his people by becoming a curse for them. This directly supports the prayer's confession that Christ bore what sinners deserved.
Paul presents the cross as the place where God is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus, matching the section's concern that mercy does not cancel justice.

sections.heading: The great exchange of his suffering and my welcome
sections.text: Jesus, you entered anguish so I could receive joy. You were rejected so I could be brought near. You were treated like an enemy so I could be welcomed as a friend. You were stripped so I could be clothed. You were wounded so I could be healed. You thirsted so I could drink. You were shamed so I could share in glory. You went into darkness so I could live in everlasting light.
theological_themes: Christ's humiliation for the believer's restoration
Healing, welcome, and glory purchased through suffering

scripture_references.connection: Isaiah describes the Servant bearing griefs, being wounded for transgressions, and bringing healing through his suffering, which underlies this section's repeated exchange between Christ's pain and the believer's blessing.
Peter says Christ suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring people to God. That captures the movement from rejection and guilt to welcome and nearness.
The darkness and Jesus' cry of abandonment at the crucifixion illuminate the prayer's confession that he entered judgment and forsakenness so his people might receive light and acceptance.

sections.heading: His death and my life
sections.text: My Savior wept so that one day every tear will be wiped from my eyes. He groaned so I could have a song that never ends. He wore the crown of thorns so I could receive the crown of life. He bowed his head in death so I could lift mine in hope. He was mocked so I could be received. He closed his eyes in death so I could one day see your glory without a cloud between us. He died so I could live forever.
theological_themes: Future comfort and glory for believers

scripture_references.connection: The crown of thorns and mockery of Jesus ground the prayer's contrast between his shame and the believer's future honor.
John records Jesus bowing his head and giving up his spirit, which supports the prayer's focus on his real death as the means by which believers receive life.
The promise that God will dwell with his people and remove tears, death, and pain connects Christ's suffering to the final comfort and healing believers await.

sections.heading: Receiving the Father's costly mercy
sections.text: Father, you did not spare your own Son, so that you could spare me. This was not an accident, and it was not forced from you. Your love planned this rescue, and your power carried it through. Teach me to worship you with more than words. Let my life answer your mercy.
theological_themes: The Father's love in giving the Son
Worship expressed in both speech and obedience

scripture_references.connection: Paul grounds Christian assurance in the Father's gift of his own Son, using the language of not sparing him. This directly supports the prayer's wonder at costly mercy.

Peter says Jesus was delivered up according to God's definite plan and foreknowledge, while still acknowledging human responsibility. This supports the claim that the cross was designed and accomplished by God, not a tragic accident.
Paul calls believers to offer their bodies as living sacrifices in response to God's mercies, which fits the prayer's desire to adore God by both lips and life.

sections.heading: Living in the victory of the cross
sections.text: Let every breath become praise, and every step be steadied by joy, as I look again at what the cross has done: my enemies have been overcome, Satan has been defeated, sin has been drowned in reconciling blood, judgment no longer has the final word over me, and the way to you has been opened. Conquering God, bring the cross before my eyes again and again. Use it to humble my pride, quiet my fear, comfort my heart, subdue my sin, and save me completely.
theological_themes: The victory of Christ over sin, Satan, and death
Joy and assurance flowing from reconciliation
The cross as God's power to humble, comfort, and save

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes God forgiving sins through the cross and disarming hostile spiritual powers. This supports the prayer's confidence that the cross defeats enemies and secures reconciliation.
Hebrews says believers now have confidence to enter God's presence through Jesus' blood, which grounds the prayer's image of heaven opened through the cross.
Paul calls the word of the cross God's power to those being saved, matching the prayer's request that God show the cross as mighty to subdue, comfort, and save.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original says Christ endured 'infinite punishment.' In this adaptation, that idea is expressed as Christ bearing the full curse and satisfying divine justice, avoiding speculation about how the infinite value of Christ's person relates to the duration or intensity of his sufferings.

The original phrase 'surrendered to hell's worst' can raise questions about whether Christ descended into hell or suffered the exact experience of the damned. The adaptation renders the force as Christ entering judgment, forsakenness, darkness, and the curse for sinners without making a contested claim beyond the crucifixion texts.

The original speaks of Satan as 'destroyed.' The New Testament presents Christ's victory as decisive while the final public destruction of evil awaits consummation. The adaptation uses 'defeated' and 'overcome' to preserve the victory theme while allowing the already/not-yet tension.

The original's language that Christ was 'made a transgressor' and 'made sin' is strongly biblical but can be misunderstood as implying Christ became morally sinful. The adaptation clarifies that he was holy while standing in the place of sinners and being treated as sin for them.
significant_interpretive_choices: I preserved the prayer's repeated exchange structure—Christ receives suffering, shame, curse, and death; the believer receives joy, welcome, healing, glory, and life—because that is the main devotional movement of the original.
I rendered 'Love lustres at Calvary' as 'your love shines most clearly at Calvary' to keep the title's central image while making it natural contemporary English.

I treated 'hell's gates closed' and 'heaven's portal open' as a statement about judgment losing its claim over the believer and access to God being opened through Christ's blood, rather than as a detailed claim about the geography of heaven or hell.
I kept the prayer in first person singular throughout, in keeping with the supplied personal voice metadata.
